title: Coffee altitudes: recording errors set to missing
text: 35 coffee lots have an altitude below 100 m or above 3,000 m, for example "190164" recorded as 190,164 m; "1100.00 mosl" recorded as 110,000 m; "11000 metros" recorded as 11,000 m. Lost decimal points and feet typed as metres are the likely causes. They are set to missing rather than guessed; 230 lots had no altitude at all. One lot with every score at zero was removed, and the harvest year comes as 46 distinct entries, such as '4T/10', 'Mayo a Julio' or '2017 / 2018'.

title: Coffee total score is the sum of the ten attributes
text: The total cup score equals the sum of the ten attribute scores (largest gap 0.5 points). A model that predicts the total from the attributes is therefore circular, whatever its accuracy.

title: The chocolate liking scale direction is ambiguous in the documentation
text: The package documentation describes the chocolate liking scale as 0 = liking and 10 = disliking, the opposite of the cocktail scale. This project reads 10 as the most liked, like the cocktail data and the package's own preference-mapping functions. If the documentation is right, every chocolate liking conclusion flips (the most liked becomes the least liked, and each segment's favourites reverse); the segments themselves and the panel results do not change.

title: The graded coffee attributes mostly measure one thing
text: On the 1,310 arabica lots, the first principal component carries 72% of the variance of the seven graded attributes (median correlation 0.67). Uniformity, clean cup and sweetness are scored 10 out of 10 for 86% to 91% of lots. A dashboard showing all ten attributes side by side mostly repeats one overall quality signal.

title: The natural-versus-washed gap cannot be separated from origin
text: Across all arabica lots, natural (dry) coffees score +0.39 points above washed ones, and +0.58 in the 11 countries that use both (855 lots). Compared within the same country, the gap is +0.08 points (95% CI -0.63 to +0.78, standard errors clustered by owner). The interval is wide: the data can neither confirm nor rule out a process effect as large as the raw gap. What it does show is that the raw comparison mixes process with origin, so it should not be quoted as a process effect. No attribute differs after a Holm correction.

title: Higher-grown coffee scores a little higher, even within a country
text: Each extra 500 m of altitude goes with +0.42 total points within the same country and process (95% CI +0.14 to +0.70, clustered by owner; 1,026 lots), about half the raw slope of +0.80. Acidity rises the most (+0.061 per 500 m). The effect is real but small: one standard deviation of the total score is 2.7 points.

title: The chocolate panel separates the six chocolates on every descriptor
text: 14 of 14 descriptors separate the chocolates at p < 0.001 (product effect tested against the panelist-by-product interaction). After a Holm correction, the panelists rank the products differently on 1 descriptor (Melting), the first to recalibrate in panel training.

title: Three panelists to check before their scores weigh on decisions
text: Panelists 25 and 6 agree with the others with a median correlation of 0.18 and 0.25, against 0.75 for the median panelist. Panelist 27 separates the products on 0 of the 14 descriptors on their own scores (median panelist: 4).

title: The six chocolates differ along one sensory axis
text: The first component of the panel profiles carries 89% of the variance: milky, sweet, caramel and melting on one side, cocoa, bitter, astringent and crunchy on the other. Chocolate 3 is the milky outlier.

title: Average liking hides two opposite chocolate segments
text: Mean liking ranges only from 5.3 to 5.9 out of 10, as if no chocolate stood out. But consumers fall into two segments (129 and 93 consumers): chocolate 3 scores 7.3 in the first and 3.7 in the second. The shared preference axis is real (it carries 34% of the liking variance, against a 95th percentile of 27% for shuffled data, p < 0.001) and it is the sensory axis itself (correlation 0.99). The segment boundary is soft (silhouette 0.19): consumers spread along that axis rather than forming two separate clusters.

title: No attribute drives chocolate liking on average, because the segments pull both ways
text: Across all consumers, the strongest correlation with mean liking is -0.68 (Acidity), and no attribute reaches p < 0.05 over six products. Within segments the picture is sharp: melting correlates +0.97 with liking in the first segment and -0.95 in the second, while crunchy goes -0.87 and +0.88. This flip partly follows from how the segments are formed (along the same sensory axis), so it describes the segments rather than testing them. A team reading only the averages would conclude that nothing matters.

title: Cocktail liking is driven by sweetness and hurt by acidity, strength and bitterness
text: Across the 16 cocktails, mean liking correlates with sweet (+0.74), bitterness (-0.69), strongness (-0.81), acidity (-0.83) (each p < 0.01 over products).

title: Cocktail liking is predictable from the recipe
text: A mixture model of the four juice proportions predicts mean liking of a recipe it has not seen with an error of 0.42 points (leave-one-recipe-out), against 1.06 points of spread between cocktails and 0.27 between three servings of the same recipe. Lemon costs the most: replacing 0.2 dl of mango with lemon lowers predicted liking by 1.2 points.

title: No untested recipe is predicted to beat the best cocktail
text: Searching every recipe inside the tested range, the model's best is 0.78 dl orange, 1.17 banana, 1.95 mango and 0.00 lemon, which is exactly Cocktail 2, already the most liked (6.98). A linear mixture model always puts its optimum at a corner of the tested range, so its useful output is a direction for the next tasting: less orange and no lemon, beyond the tested range, to be confirmed by consumers.

title: A lemon-averse segment of cocktail drinkers
text: 38 of the 100 consumers rate the cocktails with the most lemon (0.39 dl) 3.4 on average, against 7.0 for those without lemon. For the other 62 consumers the gap is smaller (4.8 against 6.2). Their favourite is Cocktail 11 (7.6), while the larger group prefers Cocktail 2.

title: Cocktail colour intensity is not explained by the recipe
text: Three servings of the same recipe (cocktails 8, 9 and 10) score 8.2, 3.5 and 3.1 for colour intensity, and the scores split into two groups around 3 and 8 whatever the juices. A factor missing from the data (a colouring, or how samples were served) drives it, so colour is left out of the maps and the recipe model.
